text:
Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is a leading cause of maternal mortality in Nigeria and in most low- and middle-income countries. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends oxytocin as effective, affordable, and the safest drug of first choice in the prevention and treatment of PPH in the third stage of labor. However, there are concerns about its quality. Very high prevalence of poor-quality oxytocin, especially in Africa and Asia, has been reported in literature. Excessive and inappropriate use of oxytocin is also common in low-resource settings.

To assess clinical experiences with quality of oxytocin used by healthcare providers in Lagos State, Nigeria.

This was a descriptive cross-sectional study conducted in 2017, with 705 respondents (doctors and nurses) who use oxytocin for obstetrics and gynecological services recruited from 195 health facilities (public and registered private) across Lagos State. Data collection was quantitative, using a pretested self-administered questionnaire. Data analysis was performed with IBM SPSS version 21. Statistical significance was set at 5 percent (p<0.05). Ethical approval was obtained from Lagos University Teaching Hospital Health Research Ethics Committee.

Only 52 percent of the respondents knew oxytocin should be stored at 2°C to 8°C. About 80 percent of respondents used oxytocin for augmentation of labor, 68 percent for induction of labor, 51 percent for stimulation of labor, and 78 percent for management of PPH. Forty-one percent used 20IU and as much as 10% used 30IU to 60IU for management of PPH. About 13 percent of respondents reported believing they had used an ineffective brand of oxytocin in their practice. Just over a third (36%) had an available means of documenting or reporting perceived ineffectiveness of drugs in their facility; of these, only about 12 percent had pharmacovigilance forms in their facilities to report the ineffectiveness.

The inappropriate and inconsistent use of oxytocin, especially overdosing, likely led to the high perception of medicine effectiveness among respondents. This is coupled with lack of suspicion of medicine ineffectiveness by clinicians as a possible root cause of poor treatment response or disease progression. Poor knowledge of oxytocin storage and consequent poor storage practices could have contributed to the ineffectiveness reported by some respondents. It is necessary to establish a unified protocol for oxytocin use that is strictly complied with. Continuous training of healthcare providers in medicine safety monitoring is advocated.

text:
In 2013, the Comprehensive Case Management Programme (CCMP) was initiated to assess the impact of universal access to diagnosis and treatment and improved surveillance on malaria transmission in different settings in Odisha state, India.

Pairs of intervention and control sub-districts (blocks), matched on malaria incidence were selected in four districts with different transmission intensities. CCMP activities included training and supervision, ensuring no stock-outs of malaria tests and drugs, analysing verified surveillance data, stratifying areas based on risk factors, and appointing alternative providers to underserved areas. Composite risk scores were calculated for each sub-centre using principal component analysis. Post−pre changes (2013–2015 versus 2011–2012) for annual blood examination rates (ABER) and annual parasite incidence (API) across intervention and control groups were assessed using difference-in-difference (DID) estimates, adjusted for malaria transmission risk.

In the intervention sub-centres, the mean increase in ABER was 6.41 tests/sub-centre (95%CI 4.69, 8.14; p<0.01) and in API was 9.2 cases diagnosed/sub-centre (95%CI 5.18, 13.21; p<0.01). The control sub-centres reported lower increases in ABER (2.84 [95%CI 0.35, 5.34]; p<0.05) and API (3.68 [95%CI 0.45, 6.90]; p<0.05). The control-adjusted post–pre changes in API showed that 5.52 more cases (95%CI 0.34, 10.70; p<0.05) were diagnosed, and a 3.6 more cases (95%CI 0.58, 6.56; p<0.05) were tested per sub-centre in the intervention versus control areas. Larger differences in post–pre changes in API between intervention and control sub-centres were registered in the higher transmission-risk areas compared with the lower risk areas. All the changes were statistically significant.

Intensive intervention activities targeted at improved access to malaria diagnosis and treatment produced a substantial increase in blood examination and case notification, especially in inaccessible, hard-to-reach pockets. CCMP provides insights into how to achieve universal coverage of malaria services through a routine, state-run programme.

text: In 2013, the Comprehensive Case Management Programme (CCMP) was launched in Odisha state, India, to evaluate the effect of universal access to diagnosis and treatment, along with enhanced surveillance, on malaria transmission across diverse transmission settings. Four districts with varying levels of malaria transmission were selected, and within each, pairs of intervention and control sub-districts (blocks) were matched based on pre-intervention malaria incidence. Intervention activities included training and supervision of health staff, ensuring consistent availability of malaria diagnostic tests and antimalarial drugs, regular analysis of verified surveillance data, risk-based stratification of geographic areas, and deployment of alternative providers in underserved regions. Composite risk scores for each sub-centre were derived using principal component analysis. Changes in annual blood examination rates (ABER) and annual parasite incidence (API) were assessed using difference-in-difference (DID) models, adjusting for baseline transmission risk. In intervention sub-centres, the mean post–pre increase in ABER was 6.41 tests per sub-centre (95% confidence interval [CI] 4.69 to 8.14; p < 0.01), and in API, it was 9.2 cases diagnosed per sub-centre (95% CI 5.18 to 13.21; p < 0.01). Control sub-centres showed smaller increases: ABER increased by 2.84 (95% CI 0.35 to 5.34; p < 0.05) and API by 3.68 (95% CI 0.45 to 6.90; p < 0.05). After adjustment for control group trends, the intervention group had 5.52 more cases diagnosed (95% CI 0.34 to 10.70; p < 0.05) and 3.6 more cases tested (95% CI 0.58 to 6.56; p < 0.05) per sub-centre compared to controls. The magnitude of the difference in API changes was greater in higher transmission-risk sub-centres than in lower risk ones. All observed differences were statistically significant. These findings indicate that targeted, intensive interventions integrated into routine public health systems can substantially improve case detection and testing, particularly in remote and hard-to-reach areas, offering a viable pathway to achieving universal coverage of malaria services.

In 2013, the Comprehensive Case Management Programme (CCMP) was launched to evaluate the effect of universal access to diagnosis and treatment, along with enhanced surveillance, on malaria transmission across diverse settings in Odisha state, India.  

Four districts with varying transmission intensities were selected. Within each, pairs of intervention and control sub-districts (blocks) were matched based on prior malaria incidence. CCMP activities included training and supervision, preventing stock-outs of malaria tests and medications, reviewing verified surveillance data, classifying areas by risk factors, and deploying alternative providers in underserved regions. At the sub-centre level, composite risk scores were derived using principal component analysis.  

Changes in annual blood examination rates (ABER) and annual parasite incidence (API) between pre-CCMP (2011–2012) and post-CCMP (2013–2015) periods were assessed using difference-in-differences (DID) estimates, adjusted for malaria transmission risk. In intervention sub-centres, ABER increased by a mean of 6.41 tests per sub-centre (95% CI 4.69, 8.14; p < 0.01), and API rose by 9.2 cases diagnosed per sub-centre (95% CI 5.18, 13.21; p < 0.01). Control sub-centres showed smaller increases: ABER by 2.84 (95% CI 0.35, 5.34; p < 0.05), and API by 3.68 (95% CI 0.45, 6.90; p < 0.05). After adjusting for control group trends, intervention areas recorded 5.52 more cases diagnosed (95% CI 0.34, 10.70; p < 0.05) and 3.6 more cases tested (95% CI 0.58, 6.56; p < 0.05) per sub-centre. The difference in API changes was greater in high-risk transmission areas than in low-risk ones. All differences were statistically significant.  

These results show that targeted, intensive efforts to improve access to malaria diagnosis and treatment led to substantial gains in blood testing and case detection, particularly in remote and hard-to-reach areas. The CCMP demonstrates how a routine, state-run programme can advance universal coverage of malaria services.

text:
Anders Fogh Rasmussen, the Prime Minister of Denmark, said on Tuesday that he will seek broad parliamentary support for a national referendum on joining the euro, the common currency of the Eurozone.

Berlingske Tidende is reporting that Rasmussen is meeting with political leaders to negotiate support for the referendum.

In 1992, Danish voters rejected the Maastrict Treaty in a referendum. It was only able to pass the following year after the Edinburgh Agreement granted Denmark an opt-out of the third stage of the Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union (EMU).

In 2000, Denmark again rejected the common currency in a euro referendum. The current currency of the Scandinavian country is the Danish krone. As part of stage two of the EMU, the exchange rate of the krone is allowed to fluctuate within a ±2.25% range to the euro.

In order to maintain this peg Danmarks Nationalbank, the central bank, adjusts interest rates and performs foreign exchange operations by buying and selling currency. To do this, Danmarks Nationalbank has had to raise rates twice, even as other central banks, including the European Central Bank (ECB), were lowering rates to deal with the current economic crisis.

As a result, interest rates in Denmark are now 175 basis points higher than the ECB's rates. As recently as May, the difference was only 25 basis points.

Rasmussen heads the Venstre party which leads a minority coalition government. The main opposition party, the Social Democrats, also support adopting the euro as the nation's currency.

While there has long been support among the politicians, the euro has failed when it has been put before the voters. However, recent opinion polls have shown a growing support for the euro among Danes. The most recent of these have seen those in favor just topping the 50% level needed to pass a referendum.

Rasmussen has said he wants a referendum put before voters before 2011. His government had originally planned to hold a referendum this past September to abolish the EMU opt-outs, but that was scrapped when Ireland voted down the Treaty of Lisbon.

Analysts consulted by Berlingske Tidende have said that an endorsement from the Socialist People's Party (SF) could prove to be the tide-turner.

Prime Minister Anders Fogh Rasmussen has announced plans to pursue a national referendum on Denmark’s entry into the eurozone, seeking broad parliamentary backing for the move. The announcement follows reports that Rasmussen is meeting with political leaders to secure support, including from the Social Democrats, who have expressed backing for adopting the euro. Rasmussen, head of the Venstre party and leader of a minority coalition government, aims to hold the referendum before 2011. The original plan to hold a vote in September on ending Denmark’s opt-outs from the European Union’s third stage of Economic and Monetary Union was abandoned after Ireland rejected the Treaty of Lisbon.

Denmark has previously rejected the euro in referendums, most notably in 1992 when voters rejected the Maastricht Treaty. The treaty only passed after the Edinburgh Agreement granted Denmark an opt-out from the third stage of the European Union’s Economic and Monetary Union. A second referendum in 2000 again resulted in rejection of the common currency. The Danish krone remains the country’s official currency. As part of stage two of the EMU, the krone is pegged to the euro within a ±2.25% fluctuation band.

To maintain this peg, Danmarks Nationalbank conducts frequent foreign exchange operations and adjusts interest rates. The central bank has raised rates twice during the current economic crisis, despite reductions by the European Central Bank. As a result, Denmark’s interest rates now stand 175 basis points above the ECB’s rate, a significant increase from the 25 basis point gap recorded as recently as May. The widening spread reflects the burden of sustaining the currency peg under challenging monetary conditions.

Although political leaders have long supported euro adoption, past referendums show public resistance. However, recent opinion polling indicates a shift, with support for the euro now slightly exceeding 50%—the threshold needed for a successful referendum. Analysts noted that an endorsement from the Socialist People’s Party (SF) could be decisive in securing passage, given the party’s influence in forming a coalition.

The whereabouts of Bakiyev's brothers, whom Roza Otunbayeva, the interim President of Kyrgyzstan had refused security was not clear. The Interfax news agency of Russia mentioned witnesses claimed the deposed president had boarded the plane without his brother. Bakiyev’s son, Maksim, is already away from Kyrgyzstan. Details about Bakiyev’s departure and its planning was also not known.

Earlier today, gunshots were heard in south Kyrgyzstan during a political rally held by the deposed Kyrgyz President. This attack caused no injuries, but Bakiyev took a car to leave the rally after the shots were heard.

Bakiyev has been holding political meetings in towns near Teyit. Thursday's rally was in Osh, the largest city in south Kyrgyzstan, where the former was addressing a crowd of 5,000 people. Bakiyev arrived in a convoy consisting of minivans at Osh, where another rally supporting the country's interim government was being held.

Aziza Abdirasulova, a human rights activist, told The New York Times agency that when Bakiyev started addressing the crowd, supporters of the interim government came running at him. His bodyguards fired in the air and Bakiyev was assisted into a car and driven away from the city. She affirmed that no one was wounded. Eyewitnesses confirmed what Abdirasulova said, adding that the other political meeting was being held about 300 meters by members of the interim government. Two of Bakiyev's brothers were in the convoy with him.

Bakiyev has claimed he would resign his post if the interim government assured security to him and his family members. The latter have agreed to make such security guarantees to Bakiyev, but have refused it for him family members. They also said Bakiyev would either have to leave the country or be prosecuted, blaming him for corruption and the violences which occurred earlier this month. On Wednesday, Roza Otunbayeva, interim President of the country, said she would consider a direct discussion with Bakiyev but refused to discuss what would happen to his relatives.

In the hours before his departure, Bakiyev was seen holding a series of political meetings in locations near Teyit. Thursday’s rally took place in Osh, Kyrgyzstan’s largest city in the south, where he addressed a crowd estimated at around 5,000 people. He arrived in a convoy of minivans at the event, which coincided with a separate rally supporting the current interim government.

Human rights activist Aziza Abdirasulova stated that when Bakiyev began speaking at his rally, supporters of the interim authorities rushed toward him. In response, his bodyguards opened fire in the air, and Bakiyev was quickly moved into a car and driven away from the scene. Abdirasulova asserted that no one was injured during the confrontation, and eyewitness accounts corroborated her account, noting that a rival political event was held roughly 300 meters away. Reports also indicated that two of Bakiyev’s brothers were present in the same convoy as the president.

Bakiyev had previously stated his willingness to resign if the interim government could guarantee his and his family’s safety. However, as of that time, the interim authorities had assured protection only for him, not for his family members. They reiterated that Bakiyev would either have to leave Kyrgyzstan or face prosecution for alleged corruption and violence that occurred earlier this month. Meanwhile, interim President Roza Otunbayeva indicated a willingness to engage directly with Bakiyev but maintained her refusal to discuss the fate or safety of his family.

text:
Dale Ogden, a 2010 California gubernatorial candidate, talks with Wikinews reporter Mike Morales about his platform.

((MM)) On one of California's major issues today, how do you propose to fix our failing economy?

((DO)) We need to roll-back spending to the level of 1998, adjusted for inflation and population (does anyone think we didn't have enough government in 1998?); lower taxes significantly (especially income and sales taxes); eliminate harmful, useless, and duplicate regulatory agencies; significantly reduce the number of employees at most state agencies; and permanently limit future spending increases based on population and inflation and limited to the tax receipts available (no more deficit spending).

We need to roll-back excessive salaries and pensions for state employees and increase the retirement age for both current and future state employees to 65 to 70 (from the current 50 or 55). We need to end collusion between politicians, bureaucrats and government employee unions. No elected or appointed official should ever get a pension or post-employment benefits.

The friendly business and low tax environment in California will attract tens of thousands of businesses and millions of jobs to California and, eventually, tax receipts will soar. However, any excess revenue should be used to retire debt or returned to the taxpayers.

((DO)) Yes. I believe in the legalization of marijuana. The government does not have either the right nor the moral authority to prohibit what substances people put into their bodies for either medicinal or recreational or other purposes. Practically, the war on drugs has been a dismal failure. Just like prohibitions on alcohol, gambling, prostitution, etc., they do not work. They push the activity underground and create opportunities for the criminal element and, likewise, opportunities for the corruption of police and other public officials. Generally, such laws are enforced inconsistently and to the detriment of the most vulnerable individuals in society.

((DO)) Philosophically, I believe in open borders. People should be able to come and go as they please. However, the government should not take money from one group of individuals (taxpayers) and give it to others. We should not subsidize nor penalize immigrants. If people want to come to the United States and California to work and take care of their families, they should be allowed to do so. However, those who commit crimes against persons or property should be either imprisoned (for serious offenses) or deported. In that regard, the United States government needs to monitor and control its borders.

Dale Ogden, a former 2010 candidate for governor of California, offered his views on the state’s economic challenges in an interview. When asked how he would address California’s struggling economy, Ogden called for a significant reduction in government spending, recommending it be brought back to 1998 levels once adjusted for inflation and the state’s growing population. He advocated for substantial tax cuts, especially targeting income and sales taxes. Ogden also urged the elimination of superfluous and overlapping regulatory agencies and a reduction in the workforce of most state offices. He stressed that future increases in state spending should be strictly tied to real population growth and inflation, with all excess revenues either paid back to taxpayers or used to retire state debt.

On public employee compensation, Ogden advocated cutting excessive salaries and pensions, and pushing the retirement age for current and future state workers up to 65 or 70. He argued that politicians, bureaucrats, and unions must stop their perceived collusion to create lasting change. According to Ogden, no state official after retirement should receive additional post-employment benefits. He believes a pro-business, low-tax climate is vital to drawing new companies and creating jobs in California, which, in turn, could boost state revenues—but only after any surplus is returned to the public or used to pay down debt.

Regarding drug policy, Ogden favored the decriminalization of marijuana, stating that prohibition has failed both morally and practically. He argued that such laws only drive activities underground, offer opportunities for criminal enterprises, and corrupt law enforcement, especially those most at risk. Ogden’s philosophy extends to immigration: he supports open borders, provided that tax dollars are not taken from one group to subsidize others. He believes immigrants should be welcome to stay and work legally, but those who break the law—particularly through crimes against people or property—should face deportation or prison rather than leniency. Ogden also emphasized that the federal government should take a more active role in monitoring the U.S. borders to maintain order and security.

text:
Israeli aircraft launched missiles at Beirut international airport and damaged runways and fuel stores. Additional targets were attacked, including 18 bridges, and a Hezbollah run TV station, Al-Manar, which continued to broadcast after being targeted, but later went partially off air.

45 Lebanese civilians and two soldiers were reported killed as a result of Israeli overnight raids and 103 people were injured. In some areas Israeli planes had dropped leaflets to warn residents to stay away from Hezbollah buildings.

Over 100 rockets were fired from Lebanon towards northern Israel Thursday, which the Israeli Army says are the acts of Hezbollah. Two Israeli civilians were reported killed over 100 injured.

The Lebanese road communications network was targeted: 18 bridges were damaged and early on Friday the highway linking Beirut and Damascus was hit by five Israeli missiles. The highway is the only route out of the country after the airport was shut down. Witnesses said that the road was free from traffic when the missiles hit.

Israeli airforce attacked Beirut Rafic Hariri International Airport in the Lebanese capital twice on Thursday. The first airstrike hit the airport runways. The second strike, which took place after Haifia in Israel was hit by two rockets, destroyed fuel tanks at the airport. The attacks forced cancellation of all flights to and from the airport and the closure of the facility, police and airport officials said.

Israel claims that at least two civilians died and others injured as over 100 rockets, including the Katyusha and Thunder 1, landed in northern Israel, including Haifia on Thursday. Israel said the attacks were from Hezbollah.

In related news, the United States vetoed a UN condemnation of Israel on Thursday. The draft vetoed was proposed by Qatar and demanded that Israel pulled back its forces from the Gaza Strip.

The turmoil in the Middle East has led to record high prices for oil, which is now trading at $76.70 a barrel.

The stock market in Tel Aviv closed down 4.3 percent on Thursday. The Shekel has also slipped against the dollar.

Other international events are also having it say on stock markets worldwide as investors are keeping their eyes on North Korea and Iran's nuclear ambitions in addition to the situation in the Middle East.

text:
Israeli fighter aircraft fired missiles at Beirut International Airport late Thursday, damaging runways and fuel storage areas. Additional attacks targeted 18 bridges and a Hezbollah-controlled television station, Al-Manar, which continued broadcasting before eventually going off-air. Lebanese authorities reported 45 civilian deaths and two soldier fatalities in the Israeli overnight raids, with 103 people injured overall. Some Israeli aircraft distributed leaflets urging people to keep away from Hezbollah facilities during the operations.

In response, over 100 rockets were fired from Lebanon at northern Israel, according to the Israeli Army, most of them attributed to Hezbollah. At least two Israeli civilians were killed and over 100 people injured in these attacks. The Lebanese road network sustained damage when 18 bridges were hit. The main highway connecting Beirut and Damascus suffered missile strikes early Friday morning, though it was reportedly untravelled at the time due to the airport's closure. These strikes have left the only major exit from Lebanon temporarily closed.

Beirut’s Rafik Hariri International Airport was bombed twice by Israeli aircraft. The first strike damaged the runways, and a subsequent attack destroyed fuel tanks following a rocket strike on Haifa. Both attacks led to the closure of the airport and the cancellation of all flights in and out of Beirut. Israeli officials stated at least two civilians were killed and more than 100 people injured in the attacks, with rockets including Katyusha and Thunder 1 launched from southern Lebanon.

The United States blocked a United Nations resolution criticizing Israel, with the veto proposed by Qatar demanding Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. In the midst of this crisis, global oil prices reached a new high of $76.70 per barrel. The Tel Aviv stock market fell by 4.3 percent on Thursday, and the shekel weakened against the US dollar. Other global markets shifted in reaction to developments in the Middle East, as investors monitor ongoing tensions involving North Korea and Iran.

text:
One week has passed since Israel responded to a Hezbollah attack along the Lebanon-Israel border. There is no immediate end of the conflict in sight as Israeli airborne, naval and ground units have pounded a wide array of targets in Lebanon. Hezbollah in turn has launched rocket and missile attacks on northern Israel.

Israeli PM Ehud Olmert claimed that last week's kidnappings were a timed attempt to divert attention from Iran's nuclear programme. The Rapporteur of Iran's Majlis' National Security and Foreign Policy Commission Kazem Jalali dismissed the allegation, denying any such role.

The civilian population in Lebanon has taken the largest toll in the conflict; 200 Lebanese civilians have been reported to be killed in the past seven days, 30 of them today. As a result of Hezbollah fire, at least 24 Israelis have been reported killed, including 9 civilians at the Haifa train station. In addition, 30 Lebanese soldiers have died without engaging Israeli units. Eleven of them were killed today in an Israeli air strike on a Lebanese army base east of Beirut. A Lebanese barracks was also hit yesterday, killing several soldiers.

The United Nations want an international peace contingent to be stationed in southern Lebanon to stop Hezbollah from firing missiles into Israel. The force would act as a stabilisation force against attacks from both sides in the conflict.

500,000 people have been displaced in Lebanon by the violence which could end in a humanitarian disaster, UN said.

A UN team was in Israel today, holding talks with the Israeli FM about a possible ceasefire agreement. However, the minister reiterated Israel's ultimatum that its two soldiers should be released and the Lebanese government posts troops in southern Lebanon before agreeing on a ceasefire. Lebanon say they fear posting soldiers in it's southern region could spark a civil war in the country.

Today, transport trucks were again targeted by warplanes. Israel says it believed that the trucks were transporting missiles for Hezbollah. The Israeli military say 750 Hezbollah rockets, missiles and mortars have so far been fired since the start of the crisis.

Hundreds of foreigners have been evacuated from Lebanon by any available transportation. Ships, helicopters and buses have been used by several European countries and the United States to ferry their citizens out of the country.

A week has passed since Israel responded to a Hezbollah attack along the Lebanon-Israel border with significant military action. In the days since, Israeli forces have intensively targeted a range of sites in Lebanon, using both air, naval, and ground capabilities. Meanwhile, Hezbollah has continued to fire rockets and missiles at Israel from multiple directions. The conflict has led to a tense stalemate with no clear timeline for resolution.

Political leaders have weighed in on the motivations behind the recent attacks. Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert suggested that the kidnappings may have been a deliberate diversion from Iran’s nuclear program. However, a representative from Iran’s parliament, Kazem Jalali, rejected this claim, explicitly denying any involvement of Iran in the timing of the events.

The human toll of the fighting has been severe. More than two hundred Lebanese civilians have been killed in just the past week, including thirty on one day. Among the casualties in Israel are at least twenty-four Israelis, several of whom were civilians, including those killed at the Haifa train station. In addition, over thirty Lebanese soldiers have lost their lives in clashes, some in incidents involving Israeli strikes at military positions near Beirut and elsewhere.

International bodies are considering ways to de-escalate the crisis. The United Nations is calling for a peacekeeping force to be deployed in southern Lebanon, aiming to prevent further missile attacks from Hezbollah and to stabilize the region. This proposal is seen as an attempt to mitigate the risk of further escalation and to protect civilians caught in the crossfire.

The violence has displaced half a million Lebanese people, straining the country’s infrastructure and raising concerns about a potential humanitarian disaster. A United Nations team remains in contact with Israeli officials to explore the possibility of a ceasefire, but discussions are ongoing. Israel insists that before any ceasefire, Lebanon must deploy troops in southern Lebanon and release two hostages. Lebanese authorities have expressed deep concerns that deploying troops in that region could reignite internal conflict within Lebanon.

The conflict has also increased significantly in intensity—according to Israeli forces, Hezbollah has launched over seven hundred rockets, missiles, and mortars at Israel since the crisis began. In response, many foreigners have been evacuated by air, sea, and road from Lebanon, with multiple countries and organizations coordinating large-scale repatriation efforts to ensure the safety of their citizens.

One week has passed since Israel responded to a Hezbollah attack along the Lebanon-Israel border. There is no immediate end of the conflict in sight as Israeli airborne, naval and ground units have pounded a wide array of targets in Lebanon. Hezbollah in turn has launched rocket and missile attacks on northern Israel.

Israeli PM Ehud Olmert claimed that last week's kidnappings were a timed attempt to divert attention from Iran's nuclear programme. The Rapporteur of Iran's Majlis' National Security and Foreign Policy Commission Kazem Jalali dismissed the allegation, denying any such role.

The civilian population in Lebanon has taken the largest toll in the conflict; 200 Lebanese civilians have been reported to be killed in the past seven days, 30 of them today. As a result of Hezbollah fire, at least 24 Israelis have been reported killed, including 9 civilians at the Haifa train station. In addition, 30 Lebanese soldiers have died without engaging Israeli units. Eleven of them were killed today in an Israeli air strike on a Lebanese army base east of Beirut. A Lebanese barracks was also hit yesterday, killing several soldiers.

The United Nations want an international peace contingent to be stationed in southern Lebanon to stop Hezbollah from firing missiles into Israel. The force would act as a stabilisation force against attacks from both sides in the conflict.

500,000 people have been displaced in Lebanon by the violence which could end in a humanitarian disaster, UN said.

A UN team was in Israel today, holding talks with the Israeli FM about a possible ceasefire agreement. However, the minister reiterated Israel's ultimatum that its two soldiers should be released and the Lebanese government posts troops in southern Lebanon before agreeing on a ceasefire. Lebanon say they fear posting soldiers in it's southern region could spark a civil war in the country.

Today, transport trucks were again targeted by warplanes. Israel says it believed that the trucks were transporting missiles for Hezbollah. The Israeli military say 750 Hezbollah rockets, missiles and mortars have so far been fired since the start of the crisis.

Hundreds of foreigners have been evacuated from Lebanon by any available transportation. Ships, helicopters and buses have been used by several European countries and the United States to ferry their citizens out of the country.
</source>

text:
Kasur Tashi Wangdi was appointed Representative of the Dalai Lama to the Americas on April 16, 2005. He had previously served as His Holiness' representative in New Delhi. He has served the Tibetan government-in-exile since 1966, starting as a junior officer and rising to the highest rank of Kalon (Cabinet Minister). As a Kalon, he at one time or another was head of the major ministries, including the Department of Religion and Culture, Department of Home, Department of Education, Department of Information and International Relations, Department of Security, and Department of Health. He is not a Buddhist scholar but describes himself as a civil servant. He possesses a BA in Political Science and Sociology from Durham University.

Wikinews reporter David Shankbone recently spoke to him about Chinese-Tibetan relations, the status of the Panchen Lamas, the awarding of the Congressional Gold Medal to Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th and current Dalai Lama, the appointment of Tibetan high monks by the Chinese government and some of the Dalai Lama's views on topics on religions and societal topics.

David Shankbone: What is this office's relationship with the government in exile?

DS: Professor Venerable Samdhong Rinpoche was elected the head of the Tibetan Administration cabinet--effectively a prime minister of the Central Tibetan Administration, the government-in-exile?

DS: The Dalai Lama exists as a spiritual leader and essentially a figurehead, similar to Queen Elizabeth?

DS: He’s a symbolic head of the people, whereas Rinpoche would be an administrative head? I understand you may want to shy away from using government-oriented terminology.

DS: What would be some of the first actions the Dalai Lama would undertake if he were to return to Tibet?

DS: What are the functions or responsibilities of the Office of Tibet in the Americas?

DS: How many Tibetans were lost during the Reign of Terror directly after the Chinese invasion?

DS: How has the Chinese government’s Western China Development program affected ordinary Tibetans?

DS: What happened when the Dalai Lama received the Congressional Gold Medal?

DS: What is the status of the monks who were arrested after the Dalai Lama received the Congressional Gold Medal?

DS: Do you know the situation with Ronggay A'drak, the Tibetan nomad who was arrested?

DS: Where is Chadrel Rinpoche, the man who selected Gedhun Choekyi Nyima as the eleventh Panchen Lama?

DS: The Chinese government knew he was in touch with the Dalai Lama over the selection?

DS: But at six years of age, it is probable he was not able to completely comprehend the fight between the two governments over who he was and what role he is to play. If they were to take him at the age of six and place him somewhere in Manchuria, re-educate him and deny him his heritage, it is possible he does not even know who he is?

DS: There have been no rumors, no words through the grapevine as to his status?

He also gave insight into the status of the Panchen Lama, referencing the arrest of monks after the Dalai Lama’s U.S. visit and the current situation involving prominent Tibetan figures such as Ronggay A'drak. While Tashi Wangdi could not confirm the whereabouts of Chadrel Rinpoche, the individual involved in selecting the eleventh Panchen Lama, he acknowledged the complexities of the political situation, particularly given the young age at which the selected monk may have been taken into custody and the potential impact on his understanding of his religious and political context.

He has been a member of the Tibetan government-in-exile since 1966, beginning as a junior officer and later advancing to the highest administrative rank, Kalon, where he has held leadership roles in several key ministries, including religion and culture, home, education, information and international relations, security, and health. Regarding the Dalai Lama’s office in the Americas, he noted that it maintains a relationship with the government-in-exile but declined to elaborate further on the nature of that relationship.

When asked about the Dalai Lama’s potential return to Tibet, Tashi Wangdi declined to speculate on his first actions should that event occur. He explained that the Office of Tibet in the Americas is responsible for supporting the Dalai Lama and his activities in the Americas and maintaining diplomatic contacts on behalf of the exiled government.

On the question of casualties during the early period of Chinese occupation, he stated that a specific number of Tibetans were lost during the "Reign of Terror" following the Chinese invasion, though he did not provide a precise figure.

He also commented on the impact of the Chinese government’s Western China Development program, focusing on its effects on ordinary Tibetans and the broader social and economic conditions in the region.

Tashi Wangdi mentioned that when the Dalai Lama received the Congressional Gold Medal in 2008, it was generally recognized as an honor, but did not indicate any significant change in political circumstances for the exiled leadership.

He expressed some uncertainty regarding the current status of high lamas who were arrested following the Dalai Lama’s U.S. reception, but had no further information on individual cases. Regarding Ronggay A’drak, the arrested Tibetan nomad, he did not provide any update on his situation. Regarding Chadrel Rinpoche—known for selecting the Panchen Lama—Tashi Wangdi could not confirm any details about his whereabouts or the circumstances of his involvement in the selection process, particularly the allegations of Chinese government awareness during that event. He suggested that, as a young child, the 11th Panchen Lama would likely have had limited understanding of the political conflicts at play at that time. He also noted that there had been no official communication or information regarding the status of Panchen Lama Chadrel Rinpoche through official channels.

Throughout the interview, Tashi Wangdi maintained a measured, factual tone, emphasizing his role as a civil servant and representative rather than an activist or scholar, and avoided making speculative or inflammatory statements about the political situation in Tibet or China.

text:
Imaging radar is an application of radar which is used to create two-dimensional images, typically of landscapes. Imaging radar provides its light to illuminate an area on the ground and take a picture at radio wavelengths. It uses an antenna and digital computer storage to record its images. In a radar image, one can see only the energy that was reflected back towards the radar antenna. The radar moves along a flight path and the area illuminated by the radar, or footprint, is moved along the surface in a swath, building the image as it does so.
Digital radar images are composed of many dots.  Each pixel in the radar image represents the radar backscatter for that area on the ground: brighter areas represent high backscatter, darker areas represents low backscatter.
The traditional application of radar is to display the position and motion of typically highly reflective objects (such as aircraft or ships) by sending out a radiowave signal, and then detecting the direction and delay of the reflected signal. Imaging radar on the other hand attempts to form an image of one object (e.g. a landscape) by furthermore registering the intensity of the reflected signal to determine the amount of scattering (cf. Light scattering). The registered electromagnetic scattering is then mapped onto a two-dimensional plane, with points with a higher reflectivity getting assigned usually a brighter color, thus creating an image.
Several techniques have evolved to do this. The young wolves prevent Akela from catching his prey, and at that night's meeting Shere Khan demands that Akela be killed and the man-cub given to him. Mowgli, despite being naked and unprotected, attacks Shere Khan with a burning branch and drives him and his allies away, but realises to his sorrow that he must now leave the pack and return to humanity. As he leaves he vows to return one day and lay Shere Khan's hide upon the Council Rock. The story of Mowgli's return to humanity is told in "Tiger! Tiger!" and continued in "Letting in the Jungle".

In the aftermath, Shere Khan demands Akela’s life and the return of Mowgli. Without clothing or armor, Mowgli storms Shere Khan with a blazing branch, driving the tiger away in terror but at great cost to himself. At the wolf pack's meeting at Council Rock Baloo the bear speaks for the man-cub and Bagheera the panther buys his life with a freshly killed bull. The young wolves prevent Akela from catching his prey, and at that night's meeting Shere Khan demands that Akela be killed and the man-cub given to him. Mowgli, despite being naked and unprotected, attacks Shere Khan with a burning branch and drives him and his allies away, but realises to his sorrow that he must now leave the pack and return to humanity. As he leaves he vows to return one day and lay Shere Khan's hide upon the Council Rock. The story of Mowgli's return to humanity is told in "Tiger! Tiger!" and continued in "Letting in the Jungle".

text:
Michael Strogoff, a 30-year-old courier from Omsk, is dispatched by Tsar Alexander II on a perilous mission across Siberia. The Tartar Khan, Feofar, has incited a rebellion, cutting off the Russian Far East from the mainland by severing telegraph lines. Rebel forces now besiege Irkutsk, where the Tsar’s brother, the local governor, holds out in desperate resistance. Strogoff is sent to alert the governor that Ivan Ogareff, a former colonel who was demoted and exiled, has turned traitor and plans to destroy Irkutsk by igniting the vast oil storage tanks along the Angara River.

On his journey, Strogoff encounters Nadia Fedor, daughter of Basil Fedor, a political exile granted permission to reunite with his daughter in Irkutsk. He also meets Harry Blount, an English war correspondent for the Daily Telegraph, and Alcide Jolivet, a French journalist writing for his cousin Madeleine. Though Blount and Jolivet travel different paths, they converge and diverge throughout Siberia, following a similar route. Strogoff is to move under a false identity, but he is betrayed upon returning to his hometown of Omsk, where he meets his mother. He, his mother, and Nadia are captured by the Tartars.

Ivan Ogareff accuses Strogoff of being a spy. In accordance with Tartar custom, the Khan opens the Koran at random and orders Strogoff to be blinded with a hot blade. For several chapters, the narrative suggests the loss of his sight, but it is later revealed that Strogoff was not truly blinded—his tears, shed in anguish over his mother’s fate, had evaporated upon contact with his corneas, preserving his sight. He had only pretended to be blind to survive.

Eventually, he and Nadia escape, aided by a loyal peasant. They face delays from a river fire and the threat of the frozen Angara. Yet they press on, crossing treacherous terrain and evading pursuit. They reach Irkutsk in time to warn the governor of Ogareff’s plot. With the threat averted, Nadia’s father, who had been appointed to lead a suicide battalion, is pardoned. In the aftermath, Michael Strogoff and Nadia Fedor are married.

text: Qiro Anturasi, Royal Cartographer of Nalenyr, had been instrumental for his family's reputation as the most reliable map-charter in the known world. Merchants and princes all sought his clan's maps, even as the House of Anturasi continued sending out expeditions to expand their wealth of information, surveying unmapped territories, making detail notes of fauna, flora and geography. The Anturasi had been vital to Nalenyr's growing wealth and rise in power. Considered a crucial state treasure that must not fall into the wrong hands, Qiro was confined, on orders and under protection of the Naleni princes, to his estate Anturasikun in Moriande, capital of Nalenyr. There, he continued to oversee his clan's map-making enterprise, training the scions of the clan into the family trade, ruthlessly subjecting them to rigorous training and demands, for more than half a century. Now, the family stood poised on the brink of a historical breakthrough event which could catapult their standing further and beyond the imagination of rival map-makers. Intertwined with their mission were the political ramifications for Nalenyr, the aggressive northern state of Deseiron, and Helosunde which served as buffer between the two former powers. Much of Helosunde had been under Desei occupation, and Nalenyr provided Helosundian refugees sanctuary and support to confound Desei designs on Nalenyr. Qiro's grandsons, Jorim and Keles, were tasked with undertakings that would take them in opposite directions. Jorim was to embark on a specially commissioned ship Stormwolf to make accurate longitudinal charts at sea with a secret new instrument. Keles was to tasked to rediscover the lost segment of the pre-Cataclysmic Spice Route, which would take him into ground zero of the Cataclysm, a region where the ancient wild magic still raged. Nirati, sister to Jorim and Keles, remained behind in Moriande to hold the fort, for stakes were high and there were many hidden players whose intrigues threatened her beloved brothers. Meanwhile, in the aftermath of the devastations caused by the wild magic, the jaecai who had not departed with Empress Cyrsa's expedition, continued the xidantzu tradition in their schools martial arts. Their best students became itinerant warriors who travelled the realms to help fight injustice without regard to political affiliations. Moraven Tolo was one such warrior. When hints to powerful cache of ancient weapons, imbued with magicks from their former wielders, came to his attention, the jaecais became concerned that opportunistic parties would see it as an easy means of raising a strong army without the necessary ability, discipline and experience to control the power, possibly leading to history repeating itself.

text:
In the world of Nalenyr, one family stood out above the rest in the art of map-making: the Anturasis. Qiro Anturasi, the Royal Cartographer, had spent over fifty years leading his clan in charting unknown lands, noting details of plants, animals, and landscapes. Their maps were so reliable that merchants and princes from all corners sought them out. The Anturasi's work had greatly contributed to Nalenyr's prosperity and influence. Because of their importance, Qiro was kept safe and secure in his estate, Anturasikun, in the capital city of Moriande. From there, he continued to guide his clan's map-making endeavors and train the next generation in the family business, pushing them to meet high standards.

Though he remains unaffected by the apparitions, he is haunted nightly by a glass woman—Albertina, Hoffman’s daughter and his lover-to-be. Desiderio visits the show repeatedly and finds its erotic displays mirror events from his own life with unsettling accuracy. At his first major stop, the Mayor’s Office in town S., he discovers the mayor has vanished. He then visits the mayor’s residence, where he has sex with the mayor’s somnambulist daughter, Mary Anne, who remains unconscious throughout. When Mary Anne is found dead, members of the Determination Police, described as disreputable, pursue Desiderio, but he escapes.

His journey continues through a series of events involving graphic depictions of eroticism, including acts that transgress social taboos. Albertina remains with him throughout, though her presence is not always visible. He lives among the river people, indigenous families who reside on barges. He later joins a traveling carnival, where he becomes captivated by the Acrobats of Desire, whose performances defy physical limits.

After a tragic incident, a Lithuanian count takes Desiderio under his protection while fleeing from a black pimp. The two narrowly avoid cannibalism on the African coast. Albertina then reveals herself and guides Desiderio through the landscape of Nebulous Time, where a community of centaurs takes them in.

Their safety is again threatened, and they flee to Hoffman’s castle. There, Hoffman explains his plan to reduce reality to its most fundamental elements, using both Desiderio and Albertina as instruments. Though Desiderio loves Albertina, he chooses to end her existence and kill Hoffman. This act concludes the Great War, and Desiderio is hailed as a hero. Yet, he continues to mourn her.

John Ulnar, a young graduate of the Legion Academy, carries the same surname as the old regime but stands firmly with the new order. Their plan hinges on capturing Aladoree to prevent AKKA from being used against them. But the Medusae betray their human allies, determined to wipe out all humans and claim the Solar System as their own. Their homeworld, far older than Earth, is collapsing into Barnard’s Star, making their invasion urgent.

John and his companions eventually rescue Aladoree. But by then, it’s too late—the Medusae have already launched their assault. They seize the Moon, establish bases there, and begin raining down gas projectiles on Earth. John, Aladoree, and their small band land on a world torn apart by the attack. They battle cannibals driven mad by the gas, then construct AKKA. With it, they destroy the Medusae fleets—along with the Moon, now a shattered ruin.

text:
Seven years after the events of Anne’s House of Dreams, Anne returns to Avonlea following the funeral of Gilbert’s father. She visits Diana Wright and her daughter, Anne Cordelia, finding comfort in familiar faces and shared history. Upon returning to Ingleside—the old Morgan house now bearing her family’s name—she is met by her five children: Jem, the eldest, now seven; Walter, six and often regarded as delicate for his affection for poetry; the five-year-old twins, Nan with brown hair and hazel eyes, Di with red hair and green eyes, whose striking differences mark them clearly; and Shirley, two years old and especially cherished by Susan Baker, who had cared for him as an infant while Anne struggled with illness after his birth.

The household becomes strained by the prolonged visit of Gilbert’s aunt Mary Maria Blythe, whose two-week stay stretches into months. Her temperament—oversensitive, disagreeable—tests the family’s patience. The tension finally breaks when Anne, in a gesture meant to delight, arranges a surprise birthday party for her. The gesture backfires, and Mary Maria departs, much to the relief of all.

The year brings the arrival of their youngest daughter, born and named Bertha Marilla Blythe—known to the family as Roly-Poly. The narrative unfolds through a series of incidents that spotlight one child at a time, each shaped by the misunderstandings and missteps of growing up. Amid these moments, Anne finds herself unsettled. After a strained evening with Christine Stuart, the widowed and childless woman who had once seemed a rival for Gilbert’s affection, Anne begins to doubt whether their bond has grown cold. But when she notices how weary Gilbert looks, her certainty wavers. The next morning, he surprises her with an anniversary gift and a promise of a trip to Europe for a medical congress—proof that his quietness had not been indifference, but burden. The truth restores her peace.

Seven years after *Anne's House of Dreams*, Anne returns to Avonlea following the funeral of Gilbert’s father, visiting her old friend Diana Wright and her daughter, Anne Cordelia. Upon her return to Ingleside—the old Morgan house now named for her—she is met by her five children: James Matthew, known as Jem, now seven; Walter Cuthbert, nearly six, whose love of poetry earns him the quiet label of a 'sissy'; the twins, Anne and Diana, known as Nan and Di, both five, with Nan having dark hair and hazel eyes, Di red hair and green. Then there’s Shirley, two years old, and Susan Baker’s favorite, whom she cared for as an infant while Anne was still recovering from childbirth.

The novel unfolds amid the long, trying visit of Gilbert’s aunt Mary Maria Blythe—an oversensitive, disagreeable woman whose stay was meant to last two weeks but drags on for months. Her departure comes only when Anne, in a moment of innocent thoughtfulness, arranges a surprise birthday party that inadvertently offends her, much to the family’s quiet relief.

During the story, Anne and Gilbert’s youngest child arrives and is named Bertha Marilla Blythe—though she is universally known as Roly-Poly. The narrative follows a series of adventures, each centering on one of the children, capturing the missteps and misunderstandings of youth with gentle humor and warmth.

At one point, Anne begins to doubt her marriage, sensing a growing distance between her and Gilbert. She dreads an evening with Christine Stuart, the widow and former rival for Gilbert’s affection—though Anne now sees that her fear was unfounded. When she notices how weary Gilbert looks, she wonders if she’s taken him for granted. The moment passes, and she is soon reassured: his silence stemmed not from coldness, but from stress over a patient. He surprises her with an anniversary gift and a promise of a trip to Europe, for a medical congress. The doubt dissolves.

text:
Affinity analysis falls under the umbrella term of data mining which uncovers meaningful correlations between different entities according to their co-occurrence in a data set. In almost all systems and processes, the application of affinity analysis can extract significant knowledge about the unexpected trends. In fact, affinity analysis takes advantages of studying attributes that go together which helps uncover the hidden pattens in a big data through generating association rules. Association rules mining procedure is two-fold: first, it finds all frequent attributes in a data set and, then generates association rules satisfying some predefined criteria, support and confidence, to identify the most important relationships in the frequent itemset. The first step in the process is to count the co-occurrence of attributes in the data set. Next, a subset is created called the frequent itemset. The association rules mining takes the form of if a condition or feature (A) is present then another condition or feature (B) exists. The first condition or feature (A) is called antecedent and the latter (B) is known as consequent. This process is repeated until no additional frequent itemsets are found.  There are two important metrics for performing the association rules mining technique: support and confidence. Also, a priori algorithm is used to reduce the search space for the problem.
The support metric in the association rule learning algorithm is defined as the frequency of the antecedent or consequent appearing together in a data set. Moreover, confidence is expressed as the reliability of the association rules determined by the ratio of the data records containing both A and B. The minimum threshold for support and confidence are inputs to the model. Considering all the above-mentioned definitions, affinity analysis can develop rules that will predict the occurrence of an event based on the occurrence of other events. This data mining method has been explored in different fields including disease diagnosis, market basket analysis, retail industry, higher education, and financial analysis. In retail, affinity analysis is used to perform market basket analysis, in which retailers seek to understand the purchase behavior of customers. This information can then be used for purposes of cross-selling and up-selling, in addition to influencing sales promotions, loyalty programs, store design, and discount plans.

text:
Affinity analysis is a type of data mining used to find meaningful connections between different items based on how often they appear together in a data set. This method helps reveal hidden patterns in large volumes of data by identifying which attributes commonly occur alongside one another. It is especially useful in discovering unexpected trends across various systems and processes. The core of affinity analysis lies in generating association rules—statements that take the form "if A is present, then B is likely to be present." Here, A is called the antecedent and B is the consequent. These rules are built from frequent itemsets, which are groups of items that appear together often enough to be considered significant.

The process of building these rules has two main steps. First, the system counts how often items co-occur across the data set to identify frequent itemsets. Second, it uses these frequent itemsets to generate association rules that meet specific criteria, such as minimum support and confidence levels. text:
Nate was all set to try out his newest invention at home—a machine designed to dress people, just like in cartoons. But, as often happens, things didn't go as planned. The machine malfunctioned, causing a mess in his room and getting his parents pretty upset. With nowhere else to go, Nate headed over to his best friend Cat's place to test out their latest creation: the Bully Blow, aka Pergophosphaticus III. This gooey substance had a unique effect—it turned anyone who ate it a lovely shade of blue.

Their plan was to test it on the school bully by sneaking some into her chocolate brownie. Unfortunately, the brownie was confiscated by the Headmaster, who, after taking a bite, turned a surprising blue. Instead of punishing Nate and Cat, the Headmaster saw potential in their invention and invited them to participate in Ebenezer Saint's competition. They had less than a week to come up with something so impressive that Saint Solutions would want to take it on. The prize? A year-long scholarship working alongside Ebenezer Saint himself.

After several failed attempts at creating Facial-Recognition Glasses, they decided to repurpose the Bully Blow. This time, they turned it into a helmet for the army, allowing the wearer to blend in with their surroundings by changing color. Ebenezer Saint loved it, and Nate and Cat, along with other winners, were taken to Saint Solutions.

Once there, they soon realized that Saint had no intention of letting them leave. His plan was to build a nuclear bomb to wipe out the world and start over. The kids managed to escape, but Nate and Cat stayed behind to stop the bombs from being sent out. They used an EMP that Cat had hidden on the bombs to detonate them early, just barely escaping before the compound and Saint were destroyed.

In an epilogue, it's revealed that Saint's memory was saved onto a computer, which downloaded his mind into a robotic body. As his memories returned, the robotic Saint headed for the exit, setting the stage for future adventures.

They use an EMP Cat hid on the bombs to detonate them early, with the duo just managing to escape before the compound is destroyed, along with Saint. text:
After Nafai, Elemak, Issib, Mebbekew, Zdorab, and their father Volemak leave for the desert, Elemak experiences a dream sent by the Oversoul. It foretells that Volemak’s sons will return to the city of Basilica to find wives. The brothers travel to Basilica, where they meet Rasa, the mother of Nafai and Issib, who is struggling to maintain order amid growing unrest. The situation worsens when Hushidh, a raveler under Rasa’s protection, severs the bond between Rashgallivak and his followers, triggering violent riots across the city. At the same time, General Moozh, leader of the "Wetheads" nation known as Gorayni, sees an opportunity. Taking only a thousand soldiers, he marches across the desert and arrives just in time to assist the city guard in suppressing the uprising. He begins to take control of Basilica’s affairs, gradually asserting authority over its leadership.

The rest of the story centers on Nafai and his brothers—Elemak and Mebbekew, who have joined them—in their search for wives. They are eventually placed under house arrest along with Rasa. During this time, Elemak chooses Eiadh as his wife, Mebbekew takes Dol, and Nafai marries Luet, the waterseer. Rasa and Hushidh are taken as wives by Volemak and Issib, respectively. Shedemei, a geneticist from Basilica, is brought along as well—her role in preserving life on Harmony’s future means she is included, not as a prisoner, but as a wife to Zdorab, carrying seeds and animals to repopulate the world.

The story reaches a turning point when Moozh decides to marry Hushidh to secure political control over the city. His long-absent mother arrives to stop the ceremony, revealing that Hushidh is actually his daughter, not his son. This revelation shatters the deception. Nafai’s group is then escorted out of Basilica, now accompanied by the chosen women and essential supplies for their journey back to the desert camp.

Moozh later defeats the rival nation, Potokgavan, which had been his former lieutenants, but he dies during a final invasion. Basilica falls, scattering its people to other cities and nations across Harmony. The story’s broader purpose, as revealed earlier by the Oversoul, was to ensure that individuals with strong ties to it would intermarry with those who have weak connections. This was meant to delay the moment when the Oversoul would lose its ability to guide humanity on Harmony, preserving the balance between control and freedom.

The brothers travel to Basilica, where they encounter Rasa, the mother of Nafai and Issib, who is struggling to maintain order in the city. Seeing an opportunity, he leads just 1,000 soldiers across the desert and arrives in time to assist the city guard in suppressing the uprising. He gradually takes control of Basilica’s affairs, consolidating power.

There, Elemak chooses Eiadh, Mebbekew takes Dol, and Nafai takes Luet, the waterseer. Rasa and Hushidh decide to become wives for Volemak and Issib, respectively. Shedemei, a Basilican geneticist, is also brought along, carrying enough plants and animals to repopulate the future Earth, and she becomes Zdorab’s wife.

With that, Nafai’s group is escorted from the city, accompanied by the women and supplies for their camp.

But Moozh is killed during the final invasion, and Basilica falls. Its people scatter across Harmony, joining other nations and cities.  

Earlier in the story, the Oversoul had explained that this dispersal was deliberate: to ensure that those with a strong connection to it would breed with those who had a weaker one. In doing so, it would slow the time when the Oversoul would lose control over the people of Harmony.

text: The story focuses on the Explorer, who is encountering the brutal machine for the first time. Everything about the machine and its purpose is told to him by the Officer, while the Soldier and the Condemned (who is unaware that he has been sentenced to die) placidly watch nearby. The Officer tells of the religious epiphany the executed experience in their last six hours in the machine. Eventually it becomes clear that the use of the machine, and its associated process of justice where the accused is always instantly found guilty and the law he has broken is inscribed on his body before ultimately killing him, has fallen out of favor with the current Commandant. The Officer is nostalgic regarding the torture machine and the values that were initially associated with it. As the last proponent of the machine, he strongly believes in its form of justice and the infallibility of the previous Commandant, who designed and built the device. In fact, the Officer carries its blueprints with him and is the only person who can properly decipher them; no one else is allowed to handle these documents. The Officer begs the Explorer to speak to the current Commandant on behalf of the machine's continued use. He refuses to do so. He says he will not speak against it publicly, but he will give his opinion to the Commandant privately, and will leave before he can be called to give an official account. With this, the Officer frees the Condemned and sets up the machine for himself, with the words "Be Just" to be written on him. However, the machine malfunctions due to its advanced state of disrepair; instead of its usual elegant operation, it quickly stabs the Officer to death, denying him the mystical experience of the prisoners he executed. Accompanied by the Soldier and the Condemned, the Explorer makes his way to a tea house in which he is shown the grave of the old Commandant. Its stone is set so low that a table can easily be placed over it; the inscription states his followers' belief that he will rise from the dead someday and take control of the colony once more. As the Explorer prepares to leave by boat, the Soldier and the Condemned try to board but are repelled by the Explorer himself.

text:
In Franz Kafka's "In the Penal Colony," the narrative centers on the Explorer's initial encounter with a complex and brutal execution machine. The Officer, who has a deep reverence for the device, explains its purpose and the religious awakening it supposedly grants the condemned in their final hours. The Soldier and the Condemned, who is unaware of his impending execution, observe the scene calmly.

The Officer reveals that the machine and its associated justice system, where the accused are instantly found guilty and the law they've broken is inscribed on their bodies before they are killed, have fallen out of favor with the current Commandant. The Officer, however, is nostalgic for the machine and the values it once represented. As the last advocate for the machine, he believes firmly in its form of justice and the infallibility of the previous Commandant, who designed and built the device. He carries the machine's blueprints with him and is the only person who can interpret them, keeping the documents closely guarded.

The Officer pleads with the Explorer to intercede with the current Commandant to reinstate the use of the machine. The Explorer refuses to speak against it publicly but agrees to share his private opinion with the Commandant. He plans to leave before he can be asked to give an official account. With this, the Officer frees the Condemned and prepares the machine for himself, setting it to inscribe "Be Just" on his body. However, the machine, in a state of disrepair, malfunctions and quickly stabs the Officer to death, depriving him of the mystical experience he had hoped to share with those he had executed.

Accompanied by the Soldier and the Condemned, the Explorer makes his way to a tea house where he is shown the grave of the old Commandant. The gravestone is set so low that a table can be placed over it. The inscription reflects the followers' belief that the old Commandant will rise from the dead and reclaim control of the colony. As the Explorer prepares to depart by boat, the Soldier and the Condemned attempt to board but are turned away by the Explorer himself.

text:
In computer science, an array is a data structure consisting of a collection of elements (values or variables), each identified by at least one array index or key. An array is stored such that the position of each element can be computed from its index tuple by a mathematical formula. The simplest type of data structure is a linear array, also called one-dimensional array.
For example, an array of ten 32-bit (4-byte) integer variables, with indices 0 through 9, may be stored as ten words at memory addresses 2000, 2004, 2008, ..., 2036, (in hexadecimal: 0x7D0, 0x7D4, 0x7D8, ..., 0x7F4) so that the element with index i has the address 2000 + (i × 4).
The memory address of the first element of an array is called first address, foundation address, or base address.
Because the mathematical concept of a matrix can be represented as a two-dimensional grid, two-dimensional arrays are also sometimes called "matrices". In some cases the term "vector" is used in computing to refer to an array, although tuples rather than vectors are the more mathematically correct equivalent. Tables are often implemented in the form of arrays, especially lookup tables; the word "table" is sometimes used as a synonym of array.
Arrays are among the oldest and most important data structures, and are used by almost every program. They are also used to implement many other data structures, such as lists and strings. They effectively exploit the addressing logic of computers. In most modern computers and many external storage devices, the memory is a one-dimensional array of words, whose indices are their addresses. Processors, especially vector processors, are often optimized for array operations.
Arrays are useful mostly because the element indices can be computed at run time. Among other things, this feature allows a single iterative statement to process arbitrarily many elements of an array. For that reason, the elements of an array data structure are required to have the same size and should use the same data representation. The set of valid index tuples and the addresses of the elements (and hence the element addressing formula) are usually, but not always, fixed while the array is in use.
The term "array" may also refer to an array data type, a kind of data type provided by most high-level programming languages that consists of a collection of values or variables that can be selected by one or more indices computed at run-time. Array types are often implemented by array structures; however, in some languages they may be implemented by hash tables, linked lists, search trees, or other data structures.
The term is also used, especially in the description of algorithms, to mean associative array or "abstract array", a theoretical computer science model (an abstract data type or ADT) intended to capture the essential properties of arrays.

An array is a data structure that stores a collection of elements, each identified by one or more indices. The position of each element is determined by a mathematical formula based on its index or index tuple. The most basic form is a linear array, also known as a one-dimensional array. For instance, an array containing ten 32-bit integer values—each occupying 4 bytes—can be stored consecutively in memory at addresses 2000, 2004, 2008, up to 2036 (hexadecimal: 0x7D0 to 0x7F4). In this case, the address for an element with index i is calculated as 2000 + (i × 4). The memory address of the first element is known as the base address, foundation address, or first address.

Two-dimensional arrays are often referred to as matrices due to their resemblance to mathematical matrices. In computing, the term "vector" may occasionally describe an array, though mathematically, tuples more accurately correspond to vectors. Arrays commonly implement tables, particularly lookup tables, and the word "table" may be used interchangeably with "array" in certain contexts.

Arrays are fundamental to computing and are used in nearly every program. They serve as the foundation for implementing other data structures such as lists and strings. Their utility stems from the ability to compute element indices at runtime, enabling efficient processing of large numbers of elements using a single iterative statement. To support this, all elements must share the same size and data representation. The valid index ranges and the addressing formula for elements are typically fixed during use, though not always.

The term "array" may also refer to an array data type, a feature in most high-level programming languages that defines a collection of values accessible via runtime-computed indices. These types are often implemented using array structures, but in some cases may be backed by hash tables, linked lists, or search trees. In algorithmic descriptions, "array" may denote an associative array or abstract array—a theoretical model (abstract data type) designed to represent core properties of arrays without specifying a particular implementation.

text:
In computer science, an array is a data structure that holds a collection of elements—values or variables—each identified by one or more indices. These elements are stored so that the memory address of any given element can be calculated directly from its index using a mathematical formula. The most basic form is a linear array, also known as a one-dimensional array.

For instance, an array of ten 32-bit integers (each 4 bytes) with indices from 0 to 9 might be stored at memory addresses 2000, 2004, 2008, ..., 2036 (in hexadecimal: 0x7D0, 0x7D4, 0x7D8, ..., 0x7F4). The address of the element at index i is determined by the formula: 2000 + (i × 4). The memory address of the first element is known as the base address, foundation address, or first address.

Because a matrix is mathematically represented as a two-dimensional grid, two-dimensional arrays are commonly referred to as matrices in practice. In computing, the term "vector" is sometimes used to describe an array, but mathematically, tuples are more accurate equivalents. Tables, particularly lookup tables, are often implemented as arrays, and the term "table" may be used interchangeably with "array" in some contexts.

Arrays are among the oldest and most widely used data structures in computing. Nearly every program uses arrays, and they serve as the foundation for implementing many other structures, including lists and strings. Their design aligns closely with how computer memory is structured—most modern computers and storage devices organize memory as a one-dimensional array of words, where each word’s index corresponds to its address. Processors, especially vector processors, are frequently optimized to perform operations on arrays efficiently.

Arrays are effective because indices can be computed during program execution. This enables a single loop to process any number of elements, provided the elements are of uniform size and use the same data representation. The valid index ranges and the addressing formula are typically fixed during the array’s lifetime, though not always.

The term "array" can also refer to an array data type, a feature in most high-level programming languages that defines a collection of values or variables accessible via runtime-computed indices. While such types are usually implemented using array structures, some languages use alternative implementations such as hash tables, linked lists, or search trees.

Additionally, in algorithmic descriptions, "array" may denote an associative array or abstract array—an abstract data type in theoretical computer science that models the core properties of arrays without specifying a concrete implementation.

They embark for Halicarnassus in Roman Asia, where they encounter several old acquaintances: the slave trader Magnus and his giant bodyguard, last seen in The Colossus of Rhodes, the magistrate Bato and the poet Flaccus. Jonathan is having prophetic visions he cannot make sense of, and is still plagued with guilt over the fire in Rome in The Enemies of Jupiter. Flavia is shocked to discover that Flaccus, whose proposal she had decided to accept, is already engaged to someone else. The countryside is full of prophets who are reported to heal the sick and cure the lame, giving Lupus hope that his muteness can be cured. Nubia is still love-sick over Aristo, whose own feelings are obscure. In the end it is revealed that the "eye-witness" to Philadelphius' (Jonathan's nephew) and his wet-nurse's kidnapping was bribed by Lydia, the wet nurse; her child had died and she kidnapped him to compensate for her loss.

text:
Hiding beneath the roof of Chryses’s modest home in Egypt, Flavia, Nubia, Jonathan, and Lupus awaited their uncertain fate. They had sought refuge together, still hunted by the Roman authorities, their anxiety eased only by the unexpected arrival of Aristo, their once-loyal tutor. His visit brought both relief and distress: Aristo explained that not only had they been accused of treason, but one of Jonathan’s twins—a child he cherished—had vanished, snatched by slavers who again plied the roads with kidnappings of Roman children. Meanwhile, Flavia’s father continued his desperate search, unaware that his daughter and the others had survived the shipwreck that should have claimed them all. 

Aristo, now serving as their protector, guided the group across dangerous lands. With his help, they traveled on toward Halicarnassus in the heart of Roman Asia. Along the way, old connections resurfaced. They met the infamous slave trader Magnus and his towering bodyguard, figures Flavia remembered from the Colossus of Rhodes days. City officials like Bato and the poet Flaccus greeted them, while Jonathan’s troubled mind was preoccupied with ominous visions, his guilt over the fire in ancient Rome still weighing on him. Flavia, meanwhile, was stunned to learn that Flaccus, whom she had considered her likely spouse, was already engaged. 

Through the uncertain countryside, they encountered many who claimed the power to heal—prophets promising cures for Lupus’s muteness, kindling faint hope in the mute boy. Nubia’s heart remained fixed on Aristo, her affections tangled and uncertain. At last, the truth emerged about the disappearance of Jonathan’s nephew: the witness who testified to the kidnapping had been bought by Lydia, the wet nurse, driven by grief for her dead child. Her desperate act had led to the theft of the boy to make up for her loss. Thus, the group’s journey pressed on, shadowed by secrets, longing, and the ever-present threat of discovery.
